# Large-Scale Evaluation of Modern Search and Sorting Algorithms

CPU-only release v1: six sorters, search, structures, OpenMP and learned-index studies. GPU comparisons are deferred and excluded.

## 1. Abstract

This individual C++17/Python project evaluates six sequential sorting implementations, OpenMP Merge Sort, three array searches, Skip List and four B-tree orders, plus a simple learned rank index. The retained CPU experiments and new held-out learned/10M/100M studies provide descriptive evidence. The new scale extension completed 600 measured sorts and 120 warm-ups, all correct. The learned study completed 480 measured query batches and 240 measured builds. This release is CPU-only: GPU/CUDA/CUB execution and comparisons are deferred, not completion requirements. No CPU-versus-GPU performance result is claimed. No universal performance ranking or significance claim is made.

## 2. Introduction and research questions

How do input order and duplicate frequency affect concrete sort implementations? How do query outcome and location affect array and ordered-index lookup? How does OpenMP scaling compare with sequential Merge Sort? When does a rank model require correction or fallback? How do separate key-comparison and process-memory observations inform timing? The project addresses these questions with deterministic inputs, full oracle checking and retained raw data.

## 3. Related work and implementation identities

PDQSort is Orson Peters’ upstream implementation at commit b1ef26a55cdb60d236a5cb199c4234c704f46726 (Zlib). Timsort is cpp-TimSort at99b612d9826e8387a30008f2b21be206181ad890 (MIT). std_sort is this toolchain’s standard-library sort, not renamed PDQSort or Timsort. QuickSort has a depth budget and heapsort fallback. Merge Sort is stable and uses a temporary vector. Signed Radix Sort uses four stable byte passes and a signed-order bit mapping. OpenMP tasks retain the sequential baseline. See docs/ALGORITHMS.md and vendor UPSTREAM.json files for licenses/hashes. Deferred GPU code is excluded from this release’s result inputs. The learned endpoint model and AlphaDev research review are documented in docs/LEARNED_INDEX_PROTOCOL_v1.md and docs/ALPHADEV_STUDY.md.

## 4. Methodology and environment

Signed int32 generator-v1 uses a fresh mt19937_64(seed); distributions and rejection sampling are frozen in EXPERIMENT_PROTOCOL.md. All corresponding sorting calls use identical original inputs. Sorting uses steady_clock nanoseconds, excludes generation, input restoration, oracle work and serialization, and checks complete output equality after timing. Primary timing contains no comparison instrumentation. One warm-up and five repetitions are used. New CPU runs use Linux Pop!_OS kernel6.18.7, GCC13.3.0, CMake3.28.3, -O3 -DNDEBUG, Intel i5-11400H (6 physical/12 logical cores), and approximately16.48GB RAM. Governors report powersave; background load, caches, temperature and frequency were not controlled. Agent-launched benchmarks and builds were serialized; external background work was uncontrolled. Historical studies retain their own metadata and must not be treated as the same session. Study protocols and exact commands reside in the audit.

## 5. Results: retained 1M sorting study

Historical evidence:15 dataset configurations;450 measured sorts and90 warm-ups; six sorters, five distributions and three seeds. These observations show workload-dependent differences between concrete implementations, not a universal ordering.
